claims.text: Superconducting behavior in the target class of high-entropy alloys is governed primarily by the electronic density of states near the Fermi level.
The overall d-electron count of the alloy modulates the density of states near the Fermi level.
The density of states near the Fermi level controls electron-phonon coupling strength.
Chemical disorder introduced by multielement mixing tunes the relevant electronic states and thereby alters Tc.
The proposed baseline is a homogeneous, single-phase alloy outside the well-studied Nb-Ta and titanium-rich systems.
Controlled elemental substitutions can systematically change total d-electron count while preserving the solid-solution phase.
Elemental substitution changes the local electronic structure, including the density of states near the Fermi level and the contributions of constituent d orbitals.
Changes in d-electron count modify electron-phonon coupling by changing the available density of states near the Fermi level.
Stronger electron-phonon coupling can facilitate Cooper pairing and raise Tc.
Depending on the local electronic environment, substitution-driven changes in electron count may either suppress or enhance superconductivity.
Increasing the effective d-electron count while maintaining phase stability will increase Tc relative to the baseline.
Reducing the effective d-electron count will lower Tc relative to the baseline.
The hypothesis is applicable only while the alloy remains a chemically disordered, single-phase solid solution without significant phase separation or secondary precipitates.
The hypothesis is applicable only when strain effects, impurity scattering, and other extrinsic factors do not dominate superconducting behavior.
A lack of a consistent positive relationship between d-electron count and Tc would falsify the proposed primary-control mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that electron-count changes may either suppress or enhance superconductivity depending on the local environment, whereas the prediction assigns a fixed monotonic direction: higher d-electron count raises Tc and lower d-electron count lowers Tc.

The boundary excludes samples that undergo significant phase changes, but the falsification rule treats observation of such phase changes as falsification of the electronic mechanism. Phase-changing samples instead fall outside the stated applicability domain and therefore do not decisively test that mechanism.
